lessons.title: Find a rule and test it
lessons.summary: Compare repeating changes and explain when a claim fails.
lessons.objective: Compare repeating changes and explain when a claim fails.
lessons.before: Make the first few rows. Point to the growing groups and the part that stays the same. Link them to the two terms of the rule.
lessons.ideas:
In a rule of the form \(an+b\), the coefficient \(a\) is the step between terms. The fixed part \(b\) accounts for the starting offset.

The fixed perimeter controls the sum of length and width. The area depends on their product, which can change even when the sum stays fixed.

Each percentage acts on the current amount. The same percentage of the larger bar is a bigger quantity.
lessons.method:
Test a proposed rule by substituting more than one row number.

To disprove an “always” claim, give one clear example that satisfies the conditions but gives a different result.

Write both multipliers and round only at the end if asked.
mistakes: The first term includes some growing tiles. Putting the entire first term into the fixed part would count those tiles twice.
Use the correct length for each width. Keeping both the first length and the new width changes the fence needed.
Taking both changes from the first amount makes them cancel in the calculation. The problem says the amount changes between steps.

examples.title: A growing row of tiles
examples.question:
Build row \(n\) with 6 tiles for each group and 1 extra tiles at the end. Row \(n\) has \(n\) groups.

Row number123
Tiles71319

  1. How many tiles are in row 7?

    [2]

  2. Write a rule for the number of tiles in row \(n\).

    [2]

  3. Which row uses 61 tiles?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Row 7 has 7 groups. Multiply 7 by 6 and add the 1 tiles at the end.

\(43\)

(b) The groups contribute \(6n\). The other 1 tiles do not change.

\(6n+1\)

(c) Take off the fixed 1 tiles to leave whole groups of size 6.

\(10\)

examples.title: Rearranging a fixed fence
examples.question:
A gardener uses 70 metres of fencing around a rectangle. The first design has width 3 m. The second has width 5 m.

  1. Find the length of the second rectangle in metres.

    [2]

  2. Work out how much the area increases, in square metres.

    [2]

  3. Someone says that equal perimeters always give equal areas. Does this example support the claim? Explain.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Length plus width is half the perimeter, which is 35 m. Subtract the new width 5 m.

\(30\) m

(b) The first area is 3 times 32, giving 96. The second area is 5 times 30, giving 150.

Subtract 96 from 150.

\(54\) square metres

(c) The area changed by 54 square metres, even though the fence length stayed fixed.

No. The two perimeters are equal, but the areas differ.

examples.title: Up, then down by the same percentage
examples.question:
A machine setting is 825 units. It rises by 40% and then falls by 40%. Each percentage is taken from the current setting.

  1. Find the final setting in units.

    [2]

  2. How many units smaller is the final setting than the original?

    [2]

  3. Explain why the rise and fall do not cancel.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) After the rise, multiply the starting value by \(\frac{7}{5}\) to get \(1155\).

The fall uses that new value. Multiply it by \(\frac{3}{5}\) to get \(693\).

\(693\) units

(b) The original is 825. Take away \(693\) using exact values.

\(132\) units

(c) Compare the first percentage of 825 with the second percentage of \(1155\).

The fall takes the same percentage of the larger amount, so it removes more units than the rise added.

questions.prompt_html:
A gardener uses 60 metres of fencing around a rectangle. The first design has width 6 m. The second has width 8 m.

  1. Find the length of the second rectangle in metres.

    [2]

  2. Work out how much the area increases, in square metres.

    [2]

  3. Someone says that equal perimeters always give equal areas. Does this example support the claim? Explain.

    [2]

(a) \(22\) m

(b) \(32\) square metres

(c) No. The two perimeters are equal, but the areas differ.
questions.solution_html:
(a) Length plus width is half the perimeter, which is 30 m. Subtract the new width 8 m.

\(22\) m

(b) The first area is 6 times 24, giving 144. The second area is 8 times 22, giving 176.

Subtract 144 from 176.

\(32\) square metres

(c) The area changed by 32 square metres, even though the fence length stayed fixed.

No. The two perimeters are equal, but the areas differ.

questions.title: Rearranging a fixed fence
questions.prompt_html:
A gardener uses 52 metres of fencing around a rectangle. The first design has width 3 m. The second has width 5 m.

  1. Find the length of the second rectangle in metres.

    [2]

  2. Work out how much the area increases, in square metres.

    [2]

  3. Someone says that equal perimeters always give equal areas. Does this example support the claim? Explain.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(21\) m

(b) \(36\) square metres

(c) No. The two perimeters are equal, but the areas differ.
questions.solution_html:
(a) Length plus width is half the perimeter, which is 26 m. Subtract the new width 5 m.

\(21\) m

(b) The first area is 3 times 23, giving 69. The second area is 5 times 21, giving 105.

Subtract 69 from 105.

\(36\) square metres

(c) The area changed by 36 square metres, even though the fence length stayed fixed.

No. The two perimeters are equal, but the areas differ.
